title: Development and evaluation of a head-controlled wheelchair system for users with severe motor impairments
author: Haddoun, Djabri, et al.

steps.title: Gather all required components
steps.instruction: Collect the off‑the‑shelf parts: MPU‑6050 IMU, Arduino Nano, Bluetooth HC‑05 module (transmitter No.1), power button, battery‑level LED, Type‑C charging port, Mini‑USB jack, 124 V battery plug, battery‑charger plug, Sochi DC‑24 V voltage stabilizer (10–36 V → 24 V), DC‑DC boost step‑up module (5–35 V → 12 V), two BTS7960 motor drivers, Arduino Uno, Bluetooth HC‑05 module (receiver No.2), 34.50 × 18 cm acrylic plate, wheelchair motors, electromagnetic brakes, and wiring as listed in Table 1.

steps.title: Assemble the transmitter cap
steps.instruction: Mount the MPU‑6050 on the top of a lightweight cap, solder its SDA, SCL, VCC and GND pins to the Arduino Nano; connect the Nano’s Mini‑USB jack for programming, attach the Bluetooth HC‑05 (No.1) with its LED visible, wire the power button and battery‑level indicator, and install the Type‑C charging port for the onboard battery. Route all connections according to the layout shown in Fig. 4.

steps.title: Provide power to the cap
steps.instruction: Connect the cap’s battery to the Sochi DC‑24 V stabilizer (input range 10–36 V, output 24 V), then feed the stabilizer output to the DC‑DC boost module to obtain a stable 12 V supply for the Arduino Nano and Bluetooth HC‑05.

steps.title: Program the Arduino Nano (transmitter)
steps.instruction: Using the Arduino IDE, write firmware that initializes the MPU‑6050, continuously reads roll (X) and pitch (Y) values, limits each to –100 … 100°, maps roll to X = 0 … 100 (left = 0, right = 100) and pitch to Y = 100 … 200 (backward = 100, forward = 200). Define command thresholds: neutral zone X 45–55 and Y 145–155 → send ‘S’; forward Y > 160 → ‘F’; backward Y < 140 (implicit from opposite side) → ‘B’; right turn X > 60 → ‘R’; left turn X < 40 → ‘L’. Transmit the single‑character command via Bluetooth HC‑05 (No.1).

substeps.instruction: Initialize MPU‑6050 and calibrate around ±45° angular range.
Read raw accelerometer/gyro data and compute roll and pitch.
Map roll → X (0‑100) and pitch → Y (100‑200).
Apply the threshold logic and send the corresponding character over Bluetooth.

steps.title: Assemble the receiver unit
steps.instruction: Mount the Arduino Uno, Bluetooth HC‑05 (No.2), two BTS7960 drivers, and the voltage stabilizer on the 34.50 × 18 cm acrylic plate beneath the wheelchair. Connect the stabilizer output (24 V) to the motor drivers, power the Arduino Uno via the DC‑DC boost (5‑35 V → 12 V), wire the driver control pins to Arduino PWM pins, and attach the driver outputs to the left and right wheelchair motors and to the electromagnetic brakes as shown in Fig. 5.

steps.title: Program the Arduino Uno (receiver)
steps.instruction: Write firmware that at startup configures all motor‑control pins as outputs, deactivates both motors, then enters a loop reading incoming Bluetooth characters. For each command, invoke the motor activation function and set PWM signals according to Table 3: forward – Right Front LOW, Right Rear HIGH, Left Front LOW, Left Rear HIGH; backward – HIGH/LOW opposite; left turn – Right Front LOW, Right Rear HIGH, Left Front HIGH, Left Rear LOW; right turn – Right Front HIGH, Right Rear LOW, Left Front LOW, Left Rear HIGH; stop – all LOW and cut motor power.

substeps.instruction: Initialize pinMode for all driver control pins.
Set all PWM outputs to 0 (motors stopped).
Loop: if Bluetooth data available, read character.
Switch‑case on character: F, B, L, R, S – set PWM per Table 3.
Call motor activation before movement; deactivate power on ‘S’.

steps.title: Pair transmitter and receiver via Bluetooth
steps.instruction: Power on the cap, ensure the HC‑05 (No.1) is discoverable, power the receiver unit, and pair the two HC‑05 modules. Verify the LED indicators show a stable connection before proceeding.

steps.title: Calibrate and test the system
steps.instruction: With the wheelchair stationary, wear the cap and perform the four head gestures (forward tilt, backward tilt, left tilt, right tilt). Observe that the Arduino Nano sends the correct characters and that the Arduino Uno drives the motors as defined (forward, backward, left, right, stop). Use an oscilloscope or multimeter to confirm the voltage waveforms on the BTS7960 driver inputs match the patterns in Table 3.

substeps.instruction: Check neutral zone – wheelchair should remain stopped.
Tilt forward – verify ‘F’ causes both motors to rotate clockwise.
Tilt backward – verify ‘B’ causes both motors to rotate counter‑clockwise.
Tilt left – verify ‘L’ makes left motor slower than right.
Tilt right – verify ‘R’ makes right motor slower than left.

steps.title: Validate performance and safety
steps.instruction: Run controlled motion tests, record PWM values and motor voltage curves, ensure no unintended activation, and confirm that stopping (‘S’) cuts PWM to zero and disables motor power. Document the consistency of signal timing and latency.

description: The proposed system was implemented using a head-mounted motion-sensing module consisting of an MPU-6050 IMU embedded in a lightweight cap. Head gestures were captured in real time and processed by an ATmega328 microcontroller on an Arduino Nano board. Four directional commands (forward, backward, left, right) were extracted from the IMU data based on angular thresholds calibrated around ±45°. These commands were transmitted wirelessly via a Bluetooth HC-05 module to the receiver unit, which consists of an Arduino Uno and two BTS7960 motor drivers connected to the wheelchair’s motors. The system was designed to be non-invasive, low-cost, and adaptable to standard commercial electric wheelchairs. This solution was developed with a strong focus on simplicity, cost-efficiency, and accessibility, enabling easy replication using off-the-shelf electronic components [8,9]. To address the specific needs of individuals with motor impairments who cannot operate conventional joystick-based controls, the present approach leverages intuitive head movements for real-time mobility control [6,11]. The increasing demand for electric wheelchairs, driven by factors such as congenital disabilities, accidents, and aging, has led to the need for more accessible and intuitive alternatives [2,12]. The system described here primarily utilizes an MPU-6050 module, which integrates accelerometers and gyroscopes to detect tilts and rotations of the user’s head, as shown in Fig. 1. Similar IMU-based head control approaches have been explored in previous studies, where the implementation of a fuzzy logic controller has demonstrated improvements in the precision of wheelchair movements [11]. This figure illustrates a series of head movements used to control the wheelchair, translating the user’s natural gestures into precise and fluid commands.
